newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel-PLO talks delayed for at least one day.
newsitem.headline: Israel-PLO talks delayed for at least one day.

text.p: Formal Israeli-Palestinian talks on a long-postponed Israeli redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron, set to resume on Monday, will be postponed for at least one day, officials said on Sunday.

U.S. envoy Dennis Ross, refering to informal contacts, said he proposed a one-day delay "to give the ongoing discussions an opportunity to develop further and create a stronger basis for making progress when the talks convene."
Diplomats and officials said the delay in the talks due to be held at Egypt's Red Sea resort of Taba could be longer than one day.
Ross, mediator in informal negotiations launched last week, said recent talks between the two sides had proved "very useful."
Israeli and Palestinian officials confirmed that they had agreed to the delay, but they differed sharply on the extent to which any progress had been made.
Senior Israeli negotiator Dan Shomron said the informal negotiations had spurred a narrowing of gaps between the sides. "It would be a shame to halt the momentum," he told army radio.

Palestinian negotiator Hassan Asfour rejected Israeli reports of progress. "Contrary to what is being reported on progress, differences still exist. There is a wide gap between the two sides," Asfour told Reuters.
Another Palestinian negotiator, Saeb Erakat, said talks with Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu's government had failed to yield "one inch of progress."
Erekat called on Washington, Israel's main ally, to push the Jewish state to honour a Hebron pullout deal signed with the Labour government ousted by Netanyahu in May elections.
The Hebron redeployment is seen as an acid test of Netanyahu's intentions towards the Middle East peace process.
The latest negotiations were agreed at an emergency Washington summit after fierce Palestinian-Israeli clashes last month in which 60 Arabs and 15 Jews were killed.
Formal negotiating sessions were held in Israeli and Palestinian-controlled areas of the Gaza Strip last week and officials said informal talks had since continued.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat pointedly hosted Israeli opposition leader Shimon Peres on Sunday in self-ruled Nablus, the only West Bank town still under an Israeli blockade imposed after last month's bloodshed. Arafat late met Ross in Nablus.
Israeli media said security arrangements to protect the 400 Jewish settlers who live among Hebron's 100,000 Arabs had largely been solved.
The reports said Netanyahu hoped to placate the Jewish settlers, who strongly oppose the redeployment, by providing them with more municipal powers.

Israeli radio said Palestinian negotiators rejected a demand by Israel for construction rights for Jewish settlers in Hebron and for Israeli control over water sources, electricity supply, and sewerage in the town.
